Instead of treating panes as passive outputs, we wrap each pane inside an isolation layer (a Listener) that acts as a secure API boundary for a Manager. ┌───────────────────────────────────┐ │ Orchestrator/Manager │ └───────┬───────────────────┬───────┘ │ │ ┌─────────────────▼─┐ ┌─────────▼─────────┐ │ Listener (Pane 1)│ │ Listener (Pane 2)│ ├───────────────────┤ ├───────────────────┤ │ [Inbound Buffer] │ │ [Inbound Buffer] │ │ [Outbound Log] │ │ [Outbound Log] │ └─────────┬─────────┘ └─────────┬─────────┘ │ │ ▼ ▼ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ │ Target Shell 1 │ │ Target Shell 2 │ └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ 1. Architectural Concepts A. The Target Shell The raw target terminal execution environment (e.g., bash, zsh, python repl). It remains completely unaware that it is being watched or managed. [1] B. The Listener Wrapper A dedicated abstraction boundary pinned to exactly one tmux Pane ID. Responsibilities: Siphons terminal output into a structured history buffer. Exposes an inbound interface to receive raw commands from the outside. Handles local sanitation (e.g., ensuring a command doesn't execute if the shell is currently running a busy blocking process). C. The Manager / Orchestrator The logical supervisor. It can run globally (one manager for all windows) or micro-locally (one manager per split pane view). [2] Responsibilities: Discovers valid active Listeners on the system bus. Evaluates state rules against the collective data streamed from Listeners. Issues execution payloads to targeted Listeners based on system logic. 2. Information Flow & Interfaces Interface I: The Outbound Stream (Pane → Manager) To ensure the manager remains performant, the Listener converts raw stdout scrollback into formatted event slices. Structure ListenerLogEntry: Timestamp: DateTime PaneID: String SourceContext: String (e.g., "stderr", "stdout") PayloadLines: Array of Strings Interface II: The Inbound Channel (Manager → Pane) The manager never interacts with the pane directly. It submits execution envelopes to the Listener interface. Structure CommandEnvelope: TargetPaneID: String ExecutionType: Enum (FORCE_INTERRUPT, STAGE_ONLY, IMMEDIATE_EXECUTE) PayloadString: String 3. Core Logic Routines A. The Listener Event Loop Each individual pane runs this logic concurrently in the background. Routine RunPaneListener(PaneID): Initialize local buffer file for PaneID Loop infinitely: Read new raw delta lines from terminal window history If new lines detected: Clean ANSI terminal escape codes and colors Package lines into ListenerLogEntry struct Append entry to global or local IPC state bus Truncate history log to maximum line retention limit (e.g., last 1000 lines) Sleep brief polling interval B. The Manager Decision Matrix The centralized agent reads the consolidated state and coordinates execution steps. Routine RunManagerOrchestrator(): Loop infinitely: ActiveListeners = Query tmux session for active wrapped PaneIDs For each Listener in ActiveListeners: LogHistory = Read ListenerLogEntry data for Listener // Execute Rule Matching Matrix EvaluateSystemRules(Listener, LogHistory) Sleep evaluation interval Routine EvaluateSystemRules(Listener, LogHistory): If LogHistory contains matching pattern "Error: Out of Memory": Construct CommandEnvelope: TargetPaneID = Listener.PaneID ExecutionType = FORCE_INTERRUPT PayloadString = "systemctl restart application" Dispatch CommandEnvelope to target pane 4. Scalability Design Considerations Decoupled Messaging: Using the file system or named sockets (FIFOs) for the IPC state bus allows you to easily switch from a monolithic manager to a decentralized manager later without modifying the underlying Listener framework. Crash Resilience: If the Manager process dies, the Listeners continue logging output and buffering commands independently. When a new Manager initializes, it can read the backlog without missing vital exit codes. Loop Avoidance (Feedback Echo): The Listener must be smart enough to distinguish between a target application throwing an error vs. the Manager running a troubleshooting script that echoes that same error text back to screen. turns.response_html:
This architectural blueprint is exceptionally well-thought-out. By implementing a Sidecar Pattern for individual tmux panes, you have successfully decoupled execution, logging, and orchestration. This mitigates many of the classic fragility issues associated with raw terminal automation (e.g., timing hazards, missing state transitions, or crashing the orchestrator when a single pane fails).

Here is an evaluation of the foundation, along with a few technical considerations to ensure it scales robustly.

🏗️ Architectural Strengths

  • Non-Invasive Introspection: Keeping the Target Shell completely unaware of the Listener ensures maximum compatibility. It allows you to wrap arbitrary interactive binaries (Bash, Python REPL, custom CLIs) without rewriting their internals.
  • Decoupled Resilience: Buffering state independently via IPC guarantees that the Manager can be hot-reloaded or crashed without dropping critical historical context or terminal outputs.
  • Local Sanitation: Empowering the Listener to block incoming commands when the Target Shell is executing a synchronous, blocking process protects the environment from execution race conditions.

🛠️ Critical Technical Refinements

To take this blueprint from concept to production-grade implementation, consider addressing the following edge cases:

1. Solving the Feedback Echo (Loop Avoidance)

As noted in your scalability considerations, if the Manager executes a command that prints the word "Error: Out of Memory", the Listener will ingest that output, feed it back to the Manager, and trigger an infinite remediation loop.

  • Solution: The Listener should maintain a strict Command Origin Registry. When the Manager dispatches a CommandEnvelope, the Listener must tag the resulting lines in the Outbound Stream with a metadata marker (e.g., Origin: Orchestrator), or temporarily pause rule evaluation for the exact payload echoed back.

2. Refining the IPC Choice

While named pipes (FIFOs) or flat files are simple, they have distinct behaviors:

  • FIFOs: They block open calls until both ends are connected. If a Listener writes to a FIFO and the Manager isn't listening, it will hang unless opened in non-blocking mode (O_NONBLOCK).
  • Unix Domain Sockets: A superior alternative for this architecture. They allow bidirectional, multiplexed communication over a single file descriptor, perfectly accommodating both the Inbound Channel and Outbound Stream per pane.

3. Asynchronous Terminal Scraping

Relying on tmux capture-pane via a polling loop can be resource-intensive or miss fast, high-volume stdout bursts between polling intervals.

  • Alternative: Consider leveraging tmux's pipe-pane command. This streams the stdout/stderr of a pane directly into a process (your Listener) in real-time, eliminating the need to poll and clean ANSI histories manually.

🚀 Recommended Next Step: The State Lifecycle

To make the system truly autonomous, the Listener needs to cleanly communicate the operational state of the underlying shell so the Manager doesn't blindly send payloads.

Proposed Pane States

StateDescriptionAllowed Actions
IDLEShell is sitting at the prompt waiting for input.IMMEDIATE_EXECUTE, STAGE_ONLY
BUSYA long-running process is executing (e.g., top, a running script).FORCE_INTERRUPT only
STALLEDThe shell is unresponsive or blocked on an active SSH/network prompt.FORCE_INTERRUPT
ZOMBIEThe underlying shell target has exited, but the pane structure remains.None (Requires recreation)

Would you like to dive deeper into designing the IPC messaging schema (defining exactly how these state transitions are structured in JSON/Protocol Buffers), or would you prefer to map out the specific logic for Feedback Echo avoidance first?

turns.prompt_text: I wonder if there is a better way to handle this. What is the simplest and easiest way to access the output of the tmux pane once a command has finished
turns.response_html:
The absolute simplest and most reliable way to access a pane's output exactly when a command finishes is to let the target shell handle the trigger, rather than forcing an external manager to constantly poll and guess.

Here are the two easiest ways to implement this, depending on whether you want to capture the output at the very end or stream it in real-time.

Method 1: The Chained Target Command (Simplest)

Instead of sending just the raw command, the Manager sends a chained sequence. The command runs, and immediately upon its completion (successful or failed), it triggers tmux capture-pane to dump the history to a specific file or IPC socket.

You send this exact string to the target pane:

your_command_here; tmux capture-pane -pS -100 > /tmp/pane_<pane_id>_ready.log

Why this is elegant:

  • Zero Polling: Your Manager doesn't need to watch the screen. It just watches the filesystem (or a socket) for the appearance of the _ready.log file.
  • Accurate Tailoring: -p prints to stdout (which is redirected to the log), and S -100 grabs exactly the last 100 lines of scrollback buffer, ensuring you don't miss anything that scrolled off the immediate viewport.

Method 2: The pipe-pane Toggle (Best for Archiving)

tmux has a built-in command designed exactly for this called pipe-pane. It pipes the live stdout of a pane directly into a shell command or file.

Before you run your command, the Manager opens the pipe:

tmux pipe-pane -t %1 'cat > /tmp/pane_%1.stream'

Then you send your command. When your Manager detects the command is done (e.g., via checking the PID or receiving an exit token), it closes the pipe:

tmux pipe-pane -t %1

Why this is elegant:

  • Real-time & Post-hoc: The file /tmp/pane_%1.stream grows in real-time. Once the command finishes, the file is fully populated and ready for parsing.
  • No ANSI Cleaning Needed: Unlike capture-pane, pipe-pane captures the raw output stream as it happens, preventing messy viewport synchronization issues.

Which should you choose?

If your goal is simplicity and speed, go with Method 1. It leverages the shell's native ; sequential execution to guarantee that the output is captured the exact millisecond the process terminates, requiring absolutely no state-tracking logic in your Manager.

turns.prompt_text: How do other tmux watchers run?
turns.response_html:
In the terminal automation world, tools designed to watch, control, and parse tmux environments generally fall into three architectural categories depending on how deeply they need to hook into the system.

When you look at popular tools like tmux-continuum, tmux-resurrect, aw-watcher-tmux, or internal orchestration scripts used in CI/CD pipelines, they typically run using one of the following foundations:

1. The Polling Hook (The aw-watcher-tmux / ActivityWatch Approach)

This is the closest real-world counterpart to your Manager loop. Tools that want to monitor what you are doing (like time-trackers or status-bar generators) run an external daemon process entirely detached from tmux.

  • How it runs: The script loops indefinitely with a small sleep delay (e.g., every 2–5 seconds).
  • The Mechanism: It shells out to tmux directly to inspect state variables. It runs commands like: 
    tmux list-panes -a -F "#{pane_id} #{pane_current_command} #{pane_current_path}"
  • Pros: Exceptionally low impact on the user's interactive typing speed. If the watcher crashes, tmux doesn't even notice.
  • Cons: High latency. If a command runs and prints output in under a second, a polling hook completely misses it.

2. The Native Plugin Lifecycle (The TPM / tmux-resurrect Approach)

Many watchers are built as standard tmux plugins managed via TPM (Tmux Plugin Manager). These hooks run inside the server lifecycle of tmux itself.

  • How it runs: They bind directly to tmux environmental hooks or run continuous background jobs registered via the configuration file (.tmux.conf).
  • The Mechanism: tmux provides hooks for specific user events (like client-attached, pane-focused, or window-linked). A plugin registers a script to execute whenever that hook fires. For automated tracking (like tmux-continuum), they use a background loop running a standard POSIX script that periodically dumps state: 
    set -g @continuum-save-interval '15'
  • Pros: Native integration. The script has immediate access to tmux internal variables without querying across the system bus constantly.
  • Cons: Heavy synchronous hook scripts can introduce input lag or stuttering to the active terminal screen because they run so close to the multiplexer's rendering engine.

3. The Interactive Multiplexer Wrapper (The libtmux / Python Runner Approach)

When developers build complex visual pipelines, automated testing rigs, or AI-driven terminal agents, they rarely write raw bash hooks. They wrap tmux inside a high-level library like libtmux (Python) or similar Go/Node bindings.

  • How it runs: A single master Python or Go application acts as the supervisor process. It programmatically spawns the tmux server under its own management.
  • The Mechanism: The wrapper communicates over the system's Unix domain socket directly to the tmux server binary, treating it like a decoupled API. It frequently leverages a combination of pipe-pane (to dump logs asynchronously) and scanning /proc/<PID> trees to see exactly what child binaries the shell has spawned.
  • Pros: Extreme structural control. You get clean object-oriented access to sessions, windows, and panes.
  • Cons: If your master supervisor application crashes, you risk losing the target handle completely, requiring complex discovery routines to safely re-attach to the orphaned layout.

Why your Sidecar Blueprint is distinct

Most standard open-source tools default to Approach 1 (for passive metrics tracking) or Approach 2 (for simple configuration persistence).

Your design—wrapping individual panes inside dedicated Listener abstraction boundaries—behaves more like Approach 3 but introduces a distinct optimization: by decoupling the listener from the central orchestrator, you avoid the vulnerability of a monolithic wrapper crashing and blinding the entire grid.

turns.response_html:
This is an exceptionally sharp way to handle state conflicts. By treating the human operator as a higher-priority preemptive actor, you transform the manager from a rigid automation script into a safe, collaborative system.

To achieve this without race conditions, the manager needs a bulletproof way to verify if a human is currently active in the viewport before it injects a command.

🛠️ The Human-Preemption Verification Strategy

Because the manager reads the history files with perfect accuracy (via pipe-pane or continuous logging), it can use a State Verification Pipeline to determine if a pane is "Safe" or "Locked."

                 [ Manager Decides to Act ]
                            │
                            ▼
               Is Shell Busy running a PID? ──(Yes)──► [ LOCKED: Busy ]
                            │ (No)
                            ▼
          Does Pane Scrollback match Expected Prompt?
                            │
            ┌───────────────┴───────────────┐
          (Yes)                           (No)
            │                               │
            ▼                               ▼
    [ SAFE TO INJECT ]             [ LOCKED: Human Present ]

Step 1: Check if the Target Shell is Busy (/proc Check)

Before looking at the text on the screen, check if the shell is already executing a long-running process (e.g., the user is running vim or top).

  • The Mechanism: The manager queries tmux display-message -p "#{pane_pid}" to get the root PID of the shell, then checks for child processes. If child processes exist, a human (or a background job) is running something.
  • State: LOCKED (Busy)

Step 2: The Prompt Cleanliness Check (Text Verification)

If the shell is sitting at a prompt idle, but the human has typed cd /var/log/ without hitting Enter yet, the pane history file will reflect this unexecuted text.

  • The Mechanism: The manager maintains a record of the last command it sent and what the resulting shell prompt should look like. It reads the very last line of the pane's history file.
  • The Rule: If the last line contains anything other than the standard, clean shell prompt (e.g., user@host:~$ ), it means the human has dirty text sitting in the buffer.
  • State: LOCKED (Human Activity)

🎨 Implementation: Locking and Highlighting

When the manager detects that a pane is LOCKED, it needs to flag it visually so the human knows the automation has backed off, and it must reject any automated CommandEnvelope queued for it.

1. Visual Highlighting via tmux

tmux allows you to dynamically alter the border colors or style of specific panes via its CLI API. When a pane enters a LOCKED state due to human presence, the manager can execute:

# Highlight the active human pane with a distinct border color (e.g., Yellow/Orange)
tmux select-pane -t %1 -P 'pane-border-style=fg=yellow,pane-active-border-style=fg=gold'

Once the human clears the prompt or the pane becomes clean again, the manager restores the default layout style:

# Restore standard operational styling
tmux select-pane -t %1 -P 'pane-border-style=default,pane-active-border-style=default'

2. The Isolation Guard Logic

Inside the Manager Decision Matrix, the execution routine must evaluate this cleanliness rule right before sending the command envelope:

def execute_command_safely(pane_id, command_string):
    # 1. Inspect the latest log file lines
    last_line = read_last_line_of_history(pane_id)
    
    # 2. Verify if the line is purely an empty environment prompt
    if not is_prompt_clean(last_line):
        # Trigger UI highlight for human visual cue
        apply_tmux_human_lock_style(pane_id)
        log_warning(f"Pane {pane_id} is currently off-limits. Human input detected.")
        return False # Abort execution safely
        
    # 3. Safe to proceed
    clear_tmux_lock_style(pane_id)
    inject_tmux_command(pane_id, command_string)
    return True

This structural layer turns your decentralized panes into highly resilient sandboxes. The manager respectfalls back instantly the moment a human touches the keyboard, preventing the script from mixing its input with a human's half-typed command.

This taxonomy brings absolute structural clarity to the grid. By separating panes into explicit functional roles, you establish a clean separation of concerns:

    ┌───────────────────────────────┐
    │          ACTOR PANE           │ (Manager Loop)
    └───────┬───────────────┬───────┘
            │               │
            │ Injects       │ Pipes Data
            ▼               ▼
    ┌───────────────┐   ┌───────────────┐
    │  ACTION PANE  │   │  OUTPUT PANE  │ (Visual Only)
    └───────────────┘   └───────────────┘

Here is how these three roles map perfectly to your architecture:

1. The Actor Pane (The Core Manager)

This is where the Orchestrator loop lives. It does not run operational application code; instead, it runs the logic engine that parses state and makes tactical decisions.

  • Input: Consumes the formatted history streams from all other panes.
  • Output: Dispatches execution commands to Action Panes or controls the UI layout.

2. The Action Pane (The Command-Listener Pair)

These are your classic bidirectional interactive terminal windows (e.g., standard shells).

  • Behavior: They are subject to the Human Preemption Guard. If a human types in them, they instantly lock out the Actor Pane and change border colors.
  • Flow: The Actor Pane can inject input, and the pane's internal Listener captures both the command and the target shell's response to update the global history log.

3. The Output Pane (The Stream Reader)

These are passive viewports. They provide visual context for the operator (e.g., streaming live system logs, custom data UI layouts, or micro-service metrics dashboards).

  • Behavior: They are permanently off-limits to command injections from both the Actor and the human.
  • Flow: They simply tail a file, read from a named pipe (FIFO), or display the output of a continuous process (like a live tail -f /var/log/syslog). They require zero terminal input management or prompt-cleanliness checks because they are architecturally immutable.

Why this Triumvirate Works So Well

By designating Output Panes early on, you save immense processing power. The Actor Pane knows it never has to waste cycles checking a /proc process tree or scanning for a clean prompt line on an Output Pane—it simply reads the stream data if needed and skips the safety matrix entirely.

This establishes a bulletproof framework. Where should we look next—formalizing how the Actor Pane discovers which role a new pane has been assigned on the system bus, or drafting the initial file-based layout structure for this three-pane setup?

Exactly. You are building a dedicated container vehicle—an empty, high-readiness rig. By separating the layout initialization from the logic engine, you ensure that you can swap out the driver (a simple Bash script orchestrator, a Python state machine, or an advanced LLM/AI agent platform) without changing how the terminal infrastructure behaves.

To keep this completely isolated from your day-to-day tmux usage, the shell script should launch a dedicated, named tmux session using a custom configuration. This prevents it from colliding with your global ~/.tmux.conf or standard workflows.

Here is a blueprint for a standalone startup script (launch_framework.sh) that builds the infrastructure, applies the roles, and colors the environment cleanly.

The Architecture Setup (launch_framework.sh)

This script handles the heavy lifting: initializing the layout, provisioning the background logging listeners, assigning the roles via environmental variables, and styling the panes visually.

#!/usr/bin/env bash

# Strict execution flags
set -euo pipefail

SESSION_NAME="actor_framework"
LOG_DIR="/tmp/tmux_framework"

# 1. Clean and initialize communication buffers
rm -rf "$LOG_DIR"
mkdir -p "$LOG_DIR"

# Ensure sockets or stream logs exist for output panes
touch "$LOG_DIR/output_stream.log"

# 2. Start the base tmux session, naming the first pane the "Actor"
# We unbind default styles to keep this session distinct
tmux new-session -d -s "$SESSION_NAME" -n "Workspace" \
  "export PANE_ROLE=ACTOR; exec fish"

# Extract the unique pane ID for the Actor
ACTOR_PANE=$(tmux display-message -p '#{pane_id}')

# 3. Split the window to create the Action and Output areas
# Top split for active command injection
tmux split-window -h -t "$SESSION_NAME:0" \
  "export PANE_ROLE=ACTION; exec fish"
ACTION_PANE=$(tmux display-message -p '#{pane_id}')

# Bottom split underneath the Action Pane for passive visual data
tmux split-window -v -t "$ACTION_PANE" \
  "export PANE_ROLE=OUTPUT; clear; echo '=== Passive Stream Output ==='; tail -f $LOG_DIR/output_stream.log"
OUTPUT_PANE=$(tmux display-message -p '#{pane_id}')

# 4. Syntactic Sugar & Visual Separation (Border Styling)
# Actor: Green (Control), Action: Default/Blue, Output: Muted Gray
tmux select-pane -t "$ACTOR_PANE" -T "Actor (Manager Platform)"
tmux select-pane -t "$ACTION_PANE" -T "Action (Human / Agent Command Interface)"
tmux select-pane -t "$OUTPUT_PANE" -T "Output (Passive Log/UI Stream)"

# Dynamic borders to visually flag the ecosystem roles
tmux set-option -t "$SESSION_NAME" pane-border-status top
tmux set-option -t "$SESSION_NAME" pane-border-style "fg=colour239"
tmux set-option -t "$SESSION_NAME" pane-active-border-style "fg=colour39"

# 5. Initialize the Background Listeners
# Fire up background tasks that track pane outputs cleanly
tmux pipe-pane -t "$ACTION_PANE" "cat > $LOG_DIR/action_pane.raw.log"

# 6. Drop the human operator directly into the Actor pane to take the helm or launch the script
tmux select-pane -t "$ACTOR_PANE"
tmux attach-session -t "$SESSION_NAME"

The Resulting Structural Blueprint

When you run this script, it generates a perfectly proportioned, role-isolated control center:

┌───────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┐
│                               │                               │
│                               │      ACTION PANE              │
│                               │      (Bidirectional Shell)    │
│                               │      Border: Dynamic Status   │
│      ACTOR PANE               │                               │
│      (The Logic Core Engine)  ├───────────────────────────────┤
│      Border: Green            │                               │
│                               │      OUTPUT PANE              │
│                               │      (Passive Stream View)    │
│                               │      Border: Muted Gray       │
│                               │                               │
└───────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────┘

Why This Fits the Framework Perfectly

  1. Environmental Identity: By exporting PANE_ROLE inside each shell initialization step, any script or agent running inside the layout can run a quick echo $PANE_ROLE to discover instantly where it sits in the hierarchy.
  2. Zero Pollution: Your global tmux sessions remain untouched. This operates entirely within its own named environment space (actor_framework).
  3. Pluggable Core: The Actor pane opens directly into your customized shell environment. If you write a Python agent orchestrator later, you can run it inside the Actor pane, and it will immediately have access to read /tmp/tmux_framework/action_pane.raw.log and inject commands cleanly right next door.

Architectural Blueprint: Wrapped tmux Pane Framework

This document formalizes the specifications for a dedicated, decentralized terminal orchestration layout. The framework decouples terminal introspection, interactive execution, and passive visualization by partitioning a dedicated tmux session into explicitly isolated structural roles.

1. System Topology & Architectural Roles

The framework establishes a strict hierarchical flow among three distinct pane typologies. The target workspace runs within an isolated environment to prevent conflicts with standard global terminal workflows.

┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                ACTOR PANE                 │
│      (Logic Driver / Agent Engine)        │
└─────┬───────────────────────────────┬─────┘
      │                               │
      │ Injects Commands              │ Streams Status
      ▼                               ▼
┌───────────────────────────┐   ┌───────────────────────────┐
│        ACTION PANE        │   │        OUTPUT PANE        │
│   (Interactive Shell /    │   │ (Passive Viewport / FIFO) │
│    Human Preemption Guard)│   │  [No Inbound Commands]    │
└───────────────────────────┘   └───────────────────────────┘

📋 The Three Pane Typologies

A. The Actor Pane

  • Objective: The host cockpit for the intelligence layer (a shell script, local automation state machine, or AI agent daemon).
  • Ingress: Consumes the flat history files and IPC streams generated by the rest of the workspace.
  • Egress: Evaluates state rules and dispatches execution envelopes to the target ACTION pane.

B. The Action Pane

  • Objective: A standard, bidirectional interactive shell running the Fish shell.
  • State Constraints: Governed strictly by the Human Preemption Guard. If unexecuted text or unexpected child processes are detected within this pane, the Actor layer backs off instantly.
  • Introspection: Wrapped by a passive background data siphoner that handles stream logging to disk without polling lag.

C. The Output Pane

  • Objective: A purely passive visual dashboard tailored for rendering structured metrics, error logs, or data frames.
  • Constraint Matrix: Completely immutable. It accepts no input payloads from either the Actor engine or the human operator. It displays data sequentially by reading directly from a localized named pipe (FIFO) or flat stream log.

2. Infrastructure Initialization Layer

This standalone initialization script builds the isolated environment, exports environment identifiers into each child shell context, provisions the logging boundaries, and handles structural visual semantics.

Save this file locally as launch_framework.sh and ensure execution privileges are set (chmod +x launch_framework.sh).

#!/usr/bin/env fish

# Specification: Isolated Tmux Session Launcher for Actor Framework
set SESSION_NAME "actor_framework"
set LOG_DIR "/tmp/tmux_framework"

# 1. Purge and provision communication buffers
rm -rf $LOG_DIR
mkdir -p $LOG_DIR
touch $LOG_DIR/action_pane.raw.log
touch $LOG_DIR/output_stream.log

# 2. Spawn the parent session, initializing the Actor Pane in Fish
tmux new-session -d -s $SESSION_NAME -n "Workspace" \
  "set -x PANE_ROLE ACTOR; exec fish"

# Retrieve unique Actor ID reference
set ACTOR_PANE (tmux display-message -p '#{pane_id}')

# 3. Provision the Action Pane via horizontal splitting
tmux split-window -h -t "$SESSION_NAME:0" \
  "set -x PANE_ROLE ACTION; exec fish"
set ACTION_PANE (tmux display-message -p '#{pane_id}')

# 4. Provision the Output Pane directly below the Action Pane
tmux split-window -v -t $ACTION_PANE \
  "set -x PANE_ROLE OUTPUT; clear; echo '=== Passive Stream Output ==='; tail -f $LOG_DIR/output_stream.log"
set OUTPUT_PANE (tmux display-message -p '#{pane_id}')

# 5. Semantic Styling & Interface Titles
tmux select-pane -t $ACTOR_PANE -T "Actor (Manager Core)"
tmux select-pane -t $ACTION_PANE -T "Action (Interactive Shell)"
tmux select-pane -t $OUTPUT_PANE -T "Output (Passive Stream)"

# Enable top border statuses and define distinct aesthetic borders
tmux set-option -t $SESSION_NAME pane-border-status top
tmux set-option -t $SESSION_NAME pane-border-style "fg=colour239"
tmux set-option -t $SESSION_NAME pane-active-border-style "fg=colour39"

# 6. Bind the Introspection Layer (Zero-Lag Streaming)
# Pipes stdout of the action pane directly to the shared local space
tmux pipe-pane -t $ACTION_PANE "cat > $LOG_DIR/action_pane.raw.log"

# 7. Focus the Actor Cockpit and Attach the Session
tmux select-pane -t $ACTOR_PANE
tmux attach-session -t $SESSION_NAME

3. Human Preemption Guard Specification

To ensure the Actor engine behaves as a collaborative agent rather than a destructive script, any automated execution must respect human intent. When an agent decides to push a command sequence, it must execute a pre-flight safety matrix against the targeted ACTION pane log.

The Verification State Machine

An agent running inside the ACTOR pane must evaluate the following guard conditions before utilizing tmux send-keys:

                    ┌──────────────────────────────┐
                    │  Agent Pre-Flight Assessment │
                    └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                                   │
                                   ▼
                   Is Target Shell Processing a PID?
                   (e.g., active child of root shell)
                                  ╱ ╲
                                 ╱   ╲
                                ⚠️    │ No
                               Yes   ▼
                                │  Is Prompt Clean?
                                │  (Scrollback ends exactly
                                │   on prompt signature)
                                │        ╱ ╲
                                │       ╱   ╲
                                │      ⚠️    │ Yes
                                │     No     ▼
                                ▼      ▼     ▼
                        [LOCKED STATE]    [SAFE EXECUTE]

🖥️ Logic Implementation Blueprint (Fish Pseudo-Engine)

Agents executing within the framework can implement this safety check to govern command injection:

function verify_pane_safety --argument-name target_pane_id
    set -l log_dir "/tmp/tmux_framework"
    
    # Condition 1: Verify the child execution process tree (PID Introspection)
    set -l root_pid (tmux display-message -p -t $target_pane_id '#{pane_pid}')
    set -l child_pids (pgrep -P $root_pid)
    
    if test -n "$child_pids"
        # The shell is actively executing an active command (e.g. vim, top, npm)
        return 1
    end
    
    # Condition 2: Evaluate Prompt Cleanliness (Unexecuted user inputs)
    # Read the final string snippet from the high-accuracy raw stream log
    set -l last_line (tail -n 1 "$log_dir/action_pane.raw.log")
    
    # Define your local fish prompt match signature regex
    # Validates if the line ends exactly on the prompt character, leaving no unexecuted input
    if not string match -r '> \s*$' "$last_line"
        # The user has characters typed onto the prompt buffer but has not hit enter
        return 2
    end
    
    # Safe to proceed
    return 0
end

function dispatch_agent_command --argument-name target_pane_id command_payload
    verify_pane_safety $target_pane_id
    set -l safety_status $status
    
    if test $safety_status -eq 0
        # Restore standard operational formatting if it was cleared
        tmux select-pane -t $target_pane_id -P 'pane-border-style=default,pane-active-border-style=default'
        # Safely inject the command payload
        tmux send-keys -t $target_pane_id "$command_payload" Enter
    else
        # Visually isolate the pane via standard visual signaling (Alert Amber Colorization)
        tmux select-pane -t $target_pane_id -P 'pane-border-style=fg=yellow,pane-active-border-style=fg=colour208'
        echo "[WARNING] Preemption Guard Triggered. Action pane is currently LOCKED to human input." >&2
    end
end

4. Scalability Principles for Local Drivers

  1. Environmental Awareness: Any child script executing inside this session can query echo $PANE_ROLE to map its functional constraints and identify its context within the topology.
  2. Persistence Boundary: The history state remains safely captured in /tmp/tmux_framework/action_pane.raw.log. If the orchestrator engine executing in the Actor window crashes or gets hot-reloaded, it can instantly reconstruct the terminal state sequence upon reboot by reading the tail history.
  3. Decoupled Architecture: The system provides the pure structural layout and data pipeline. The framework relies on external agent workers to interface via the standard /tmp/tmux_framework/ file boundaries.
